expansion:
A. Restrictive strabismus is correct. The key finding is a positive forced duction test: resistance to passive globe movement indicates a mechanical restriction rather than simply inadequate muscle activation (not taken from the course material). This patient’s bilateral proptosis, tight orbital sensation, horizontal diplopia, and especially restricted elevation fit thyroid eye disease with restrictive myopathy. The lecture lists “Restrictive myopathy (e.g. thyroid eye disease)” among causes of defective ocular motility (L10, slide 10), and captions a figure “Restrictive myopathy and bilateral lid retraction and proptosis in thyroid eye disease” (L10, slide 11). It further states that restrictive myopathy causes “Double vision and often discomfort in some p[ositions of gaze” (L10, slide 19). Normal visual acuity and no pupillary abnormality also make optic neuropathy less likely; the TED optic-neuropathy slide lists central-vision impairment and relative afferent pupillary defect among assessment findings (L10, slide 20). The lecture announces tests to differentiate restrictive from neurological motility defects, but its list is cut off; forced duction is not printed by name (L10, slide 10).

B. Paralytic strabismus results from impaired neural drive to an extraocular muscle, not mechanical tethering. Although it can cause diplopia and limited movement, passive movement is not mechanically resisted on forced duction testing (not taken from the course material). Thus the positive test and TED-pattern proptosis favour restriction. The lecture distinguishes restrictive from neurological motility defects as separate categories (L10, slide 10).

C. Sensory strabismus is a deviation associated with impaired vision or disrupted binocular sensory fusion (not taken from the course material). Normal visual acuity, a mechanical limitation of elevation, proptosis, and positive forced duction do not support this mechanism. The course lists sensory esotropia but does not explain its cause or diagnostic features (L29, slide 27).

D. Accommodative esotropia is an inward deviation associated in the lecture with “Hypermetropia,” “High AC/A,” and age “2.5 - 5 years” (L29, slide 29). It does not explain bilateral proptosis or resistance to passive elevation, so it cannot account for this presentation.
objective: Recognize mechanical limitation with a positive forced duction test and thyroid eye disease features as restrictive strabismus.
